strands.code: One programming idea met for the first time, named from the course's vocabulary of 83 ideas. An idea may return later; it never returns before the chapter that introduces it.
strands.body: A body you build in GDScript: a point, a line, a floor, a creature, a field. Most of Ada's works are made this way, as a procedure with parameters.
strands.argument: A family of that body along one axis, three to five values. Before you render, you write which two members will look most alike and why. After, you make one comparison image and write one sentence it supports. The axis must show in a still.
strands.place: Where another body meets yours: you stand on it, walk through it, carry it or become it, on the desktop or in the headset.

layers.foundation: The lab: how the thing works. The chapter itself.
layers.debt: What the approximation owes or hides: pseudo-randomness, the blob look of noise, recursion that has to be stopped, polycount against smooth deformation, bias. Read after you have made the body, and from ch14 on written as a comment in your own code.
layers.ontology: The body leaves the lab: a hybrid room, an impossible space, a build that runs on another machine or in a headset.

rhythm: Decode the hall: walk the chapter's carrier hall first and guess how its work is built (PRIMM's Predict; Aesthetic Programming's Decode).

Find the family in the hall: where the hall shows one work at several values of one axis, predict which two look most alike before you read anything beside them. It is the same question the kit will ask of your own body.
Run, investigate and modify the kit or the supplied body: change one line and see what moves.

The closed exercise is the argument: one exported axis, three to five values. Write the prediction in your sketchbook README before rendering, with the arithmetic when there is one. Then make the comparison sheet and write one claim it supports. The prediction is a floor, not a forecast: when the sheet comes back less different than you predicted, look for the fault before you believe it.
The planted bug: each chapter has one real error, and you read its message before you fix it.
Make: build your own body (the project step) and carry it into your room.
Debt, after the making: what the approximation owes or hides, in one reading or one code-critique snippet of Ada's own code.
Place: a body meets yours. Stand on it, walk through it, carry it, become it.

The process strip: for an assemblage, and for any body made by more than one operation, one still after each operation with the operation named under it, in order. It is the body's recipe, and it is what you hand in. A body built with MeshGrammar gets its strip for free: the grammar keeps every generation.
The plate: each part ends on one question about the course's opening picture: what of it can you make now? The answer goes in your sketchbook, as a sketch or a still.

Decide, and say why: follow or settle. If your prediction was wrong, or two ways of looking disagreed (the picture and the marble, the editor and the exported build, one camera and another), you may follow it: change one more thing and look again. Or you may settle and build your body. Either is a good decision; a stop is part of the work. Write which, and the reason, in your field note: question, baseline, intervention, prediction, observation, another cause, decision, reason, how to run it again.

learned_from: Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook [V klee_ps]: its four parts give the macro-order (I line and structure, II dimension and balance, III the gravitational curve, IV kinetic and chromatic energy), with c4's three corrections from the text: the pendulum and top open Part IV, circle and spiral are derived from the pendulum (one chain, ch26), and the book ends in colour (ch29-30). Its Part I is a body book (bone, tendon, muscle; 'He is the scale'), and its active/passive = male/female mapping is where 'in drag' becomes a code operation: the scene tree's command chain taught (ch13), then inverted (ch21).

Kandinsky, Point and Line to Plane [mem]: Part I's steps and polarity questions (when does a point become a plane, a line a slab) become the first ARGUMENT axes (ch02, ch05); the basic plane is made, not given (ch07).

The Nature of Code [V research_creative]: its order for forces, oscillation, particles, CA, fractals, agents and learning is kept inside Parts V-VII; its midterm (ch25) and its cumulative Ecosystem Project, a museum exhibit of creatures, become the student's own hall (ch41).

Queer 3D World 2024 [V QUEER3D.md]: the three layers per chapter; first principles in its own order (randomness, then noise: ch11-12, both in the short track); the blob aesthetic and the overflow rate (ch12, ch36); scanning in week one and importing as a real strand (ch18); ChatGPT practice taught as directing and checking (ch08).

Earlier candidates of this run: c1's prediction log as QFEP's F term (ch40); c5's chance returning as entropy (ch40); c6's 'the same net is rubber or chain' (ch35); c8's 'the enum as allowed identities' (ch25) and the bias study turned on the course's own assistant (ch38).

What no comparable course has, and the course says so plainly [V LEARN]: bodies in 3D and VR that a person stands on, carries or becomes; a falsifiable prediction of the closest pair before every render; and a geometric and topological queering (polycount against deformation, the blob, the recursion that must be stopped, impossible space) that the critical-code canon, whose critique is social and linguistic, does not yet cover.

mesh_grammar.what: MeshGrammar is the project's own grammar of mesh operations (commons/mesh_grammar/): a seed mesh, a list of rules, applied generation by generation. The grammar keeps a snapshot of every generation, so a body built with it carries its own process strip.

method.name: Palle Torsson's QFEP method handoff, 1 October 2026
method.what: A proposed artistic research method for deciding when to hold an organisation together and when to reopen it: establish a configuration, observe it, make a limited intervention, inspect the consequence, decide what to follow, and either widen the inquiry or provisionally consolidate it. The course's argument was already prediction, comparison and claim; the method adds the decision, the alternative explanation and the kept trajectory.
cautions: Keep what was observed, what is concluded from it and what is guessed on separate lines.

Do not say entropy rose unless a probability distribution and an estimator have been stated. Variational free energy, thermodynamic entropy, uncertainty in beliefs, diversity among samples and visual complexity are different quantities.
QFEP is used here as a proposed method, not as an experimentally validated replacement for variational free energy; the QFE equation is heuristic.
An ordinary cause (a collision margin, a clipping camera) does not make an observation less worth keeping.
A screenshot alone cannot show that something can be passed; use a body (the marble, the walker).

plate.title: The plate
plate.what: The course opens with one picture and returns to it at the end of every part: plate 31 of Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904), Cyrtoidea, nine radiolarian shells. Read as rules it is one body with about ten numbers, shown nine times: a family on a comparison sheet.
plate.citation: Ernst Haeckel and Adolf Giltsch, Kunstformen der Natur, Tafel 31, Cyrtoidea (Flaschenstrahlinge), 1904. Public domain.
plate.lineage: Haeckel drew the forms. D'Arcy Thompson (On Growth and Form, 1917) read a form as a diagram of forces and turned one form into another by transforming its grid. Turing (The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis, 1952) asked whether a rule could grow them; his student Bernard Richards solved the equations on a sphere and matched radiolaria Haeckel drew for the Challenger report. Palle Torsson takes Turing as the project's muse. The three are the course's three ways of working: decode, transform, grow.
plate.remake: commons/artifacts/cyrtoid_by_rule/ (lookup cyrtoid_by_rule; axes form and stage). Two rules were added to the mesh grammar for it on 2026-10-01: MeshData.create_lathe and CellInsetOp. Gate: commons/testing/probe_lathe_cells.gd.
plate.question: What of the plate can you make now?
plate.not_reached: The remake's wall is a sheet with no thickness, its pores are hexagons where the plate has rounded holes, its feet are straight, and it has no wings. Each is a rule the project does not have yet.

dna.method: The hall shows the family, the kit makes one. Where a chapter's hall holds a work with a declared axis, the hall shows that work at three to five values of the axis, side by side, and the first step of the lesson is to predict the closest pair there. The kit then sweeps an axis on the student's own body with the same sheet. A hall marked 'at its default' holds the work but not yet its family: adding the sibling tokens (name#axis:value) is the integration.

title: The Sketchbook in Drag: a grammar of bodies
subtitle: Place, join, extrude, articulate, repeat, vary, surface, move, disturb, displace, grow, deform, combine, learn, release: the operations of form in Ada's order, each part closed by an assemblage
state: v2, refined by hand on 2026-10-01 from the auto-research winner (d2_ada_first, course_v1.json): the same 41 chapters reordered into the spine's order of form operations, three assemblage chapters added, one chapter split; then two operations (extrude, displace), a process strip per assemblage, and the project's MeshGrammar as the tool behind both. A proposal: no tutorial, kit, spine or curriculum.json changed.
state_detail: Palle, 2026-10-01: 'refine this order to make it possible to introduce capacity to make different assemblages or forms in logical Ada order'. v1 followed Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook for its first 30 chapters; v2 keeps Klee only where the spine already agrees (the point on a walk is the primitives sequence) and otherwise follows the spine, so that every part adds operations to one growing toolkit and ends by composing them.
principle: Every chapter adds one operation of form to the student's toolkit (place, join, articulate, repeat, vary, surface, move, disturb, grow, deform, combine, learn), in the order Ada's spine puts them; and every part ends in an assemblage, a body composed from the operations learned so far, made of parts of different origin. The spine's order is the order of operations; a chapter that returns to an earlier sequence says it is a return. The capacity the course builds is the capacity to make different assemblages: by the end the student can make a body by any of the operations and compose them.
thesis: This course walks the way Paul Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook walks, the book Ada's own research plan says it wants to put 'in drag, in VR'. A point goes for a walk and becomes a line; the line closes into a plane you can stand on; the plane repeats and becomes structure; chance disturbs the structure and, given a memory, becomes ground; the body gets joints, becomes a family, stands, falls along a curve, swings, sounds and glows, and the book ends in colour. Where Klee stops, the course follows Ada's spine out of the sketchbook and says so. Every chapter also carries one of five verbs (repeat, transform, parameterize, visualize, simulate), so you can always say what your code is doing to form, and each verb needs the one before it: disorder is invisible without a grid, a family needs a class, a simulation needs all of these. The programming ideas arrive when a body needs them: a point needs a variable, a line a function, a walk a list, a floor a loop, a family a class, a balance physics, a curve your own gravity, a swing sine. In every chapter you build a body in GDScript, vary it along one axis, write down before rendering which two variants will look most alike, defend one sentence with the picture, ask what the approximation owes or hides, and then stand on the body, carry it, walk through it or become it. 'In drag' names an operation in the code: Klee maps active, medial and passive onto brain, tendon and bone and onto male and female, and the scene tree does the same with parent and child. You will learn that hierarchy, and then make the passive end drive.

parts.title: Place and join (primitives; Klee I.1-4)
parts.promise: You can put a body where you say, give it size and a boundary, carry it, join two into a line, keep a walk as a record, close the record into a plane you can stand on, pull the plane up into a solid, and ship a build.
parts.plate_now: The outline: one half of a shell as a recorded line, from the horn to the lip, and the axis beside it. With the turn handed to you as one function, a solid vase with joints (stage: profile, turned).

parts.title: Articulate (transformation)
parts.promise: You can nest parts into one body with pivots, move the whole and keep the parts' relations while it moves: the first assemblage.
parts.plate_now: The joints as parts under one root: head, chest, belly. And Thompson's move: shift the points of one profile and the helmet becomes the flask.

parts.title: Repeat and vary (arrays; the family; Melencolia)
parts.promise: You can make many from one by a rule, turn a body into a family with named parameters, tune it live, measure what a value costs, and let a scanned body join the family: the second assemblage.
parts.plate_now: Counting round the axis: three feet, eighteen teeth. Then the shell as one class with its numbers, and the plate as a comparison sheet of one family (form).

parts.title: Surface (colour, tiling)
parts.promise: You can give any body a colour system and a patterned skin by rule, and dress the assemblage so that the seam between made and found stays visible.
parts.plate_now: The pores: cells of six, opened, wider toward the mouth; bone white on black. Here the vase becomes a skeleton (stage: pored).

parts.title: Move by law (change, forces, form finding, waves)
parts.promise: You can write motion as steps, give a region its own law, open the walker you have used since day one, balance a body, make legs that follow, climb a spiral and hear a swing: bodies that move by rules you wrote.
parts.plate_now: Feet that curve, drawn as a path made of steps. A shell that sinks and drifts under a force you wrote.

parts.title: Disturb, field, skin (randomness, noise, shaders)
parts.promise: You can let chance in with a seed, make ground from a field that remembers its neighbour, bend any body with that field, write a skin per pixel, and assemble a round someone can lose: the midterm.
parts.plate_now: Bristles from a seeded chance (stage: bristled). Pores whose size follows a noise field, as on the large shell in the middle of the plate. A shader for the engraved line.

parts.title: Grow by rule (cellular automata, fractals, L-systems, procedural generation)
parts.promise: You can grow bodies from rules in time, from recursion and from grammars, keep a genome as a file, generate a world and navigate it, and join grown bodies to made ones.
parts.plate_now: Turing's question: do not place the pores and spines; let a rule decide where they come, and open and branch what it marks. One individual saved as a file of numbers.

parts.title: Deform, imply, combine, flock (soft bodies, isosurfaces, boolean surfaces, swarms)
parts.promise: You can make bodies that give, bodies with no vertices until asked, bodies combined by union and subtraction, and bodies that move as a crowd.
parts.plate_now: A wall with thickness, and pores made by taking away. Many shells drifting together.

parts.title: Learn, break, measure, release (machine learning, graph theory, the crises, QFEP, post-crisis)
parts.promise: You can make a body that learns and say whose data taught it, a space that holds from one standpoint only, measure your own predictions, and release your hall: the final assemblage.
parts.plate_now: A hall of shells in the collective museum, each with its numbers shown, and what the plate hides said beside it.

chapters.title: Day Zero: the instruction is the work
chapters.body: A LeWitt location drawing turned into one body: in the supplied base.tscn (floor, camera, light, Label3D) you type one line that calls a supplied place_at(where), and a cube appears at 'corner', 'midpoint' or 'centre'; one print() writes your instruction to the Output panel.

argument.axis: wording of the instruction
argument.predict: 'midpoint' and 'centre' will look most alike from the fixed camera: on a square floor both land on the middle line, and they differ only if 'midpoint' is read as the midpoint of an edge, which is exactly the ambiguity. 'somewhere near the middle' will not run at all: the helper refuses an unknown word with an error.
argument.claim: An instruction a partner can interpret is not one the engine can run: ambiguity shows up as an error, not as a variation.

chapters.debt: LeWitt's drafters interpreted; the engine refuses. Literalness is the price of repeatability, the course's first debt. GDScript's English keywords are programming's default language (Marino on FLOW-MATIC), a cheap first question for Swedish-speaking students.

chapters.body: A point built in _ready(): a MeshInstance3D whose SphereMesh radius is a variable, placed by setting its position property; then three points by hand, and a Label3D beside them that counts the frames the engine has called you for (Point Zero's frame counter).

argument.axis: point radius seen from 2 m
argument.predict: 0.01 and 0.05 will look most alike: at 2 m both subtend under 1.5 degrees, a few pixels, and read as dots. 1.0 stops being a point and reads as a body; 0.25 is the one that changes category as you walk.
argument.claim: A point is a relation between size and viewing distance: Kandinsky's point becomes a plane when it grows.

chapters.debt: Mathematically a point has no extent; to be seen it needs a mesh of hundreds of triangles. The engine can show a point only by lying about its size, the first approximation of the course. And the frame counter counts frames, not seconds: in a 90 Hz headset it runs 1.5 times faster than at 60 Hz on the desktop. The repair (delta) is held back to ch13 and named there.

chapters.body: Your walked outline from ch07, pulled up by a height into a solid. For every edge of the outline, a wall of two triangles between the edge and its copy above; the fan you already have is the top cap, and the same fan wound the other way is the bottom. A second number, the taper, scales the upper outline toward its centre: 1 gives a prism, 0 a pyramid. One function of your own, extrude(outline, height, taper), returns the mesh, and a collider made from it lets a body stand on top of your walk. Then the same move as the project makes it: a supplied function hands your solid to MeshGrammar, which pushes its upward faces out again by a distance and a scale, the same two numbers, and returns a spire.

argument.axis: taper of the upper outline, same walk and height
argument.predict: Seen from the side, 1.0 and 0.6 will look most alike: both are flat-topped blocks, and only the slope of the walls differs. 0.0 is the odd one: the top cap has no area and the solid ends in a point. argument.claim: One outline and two numbers make a family of solids; the cube of the next chapter is this function called with a square and a taper of 1.

chapters.debt: An extrusion remembers only its outline. Every wall is flat, every section has the same shape, and the solid cannot bulge, lean or twist: it is the default body of drawing software, and most buildings on a screen are extrusions of their plan. The walls also want their own normals, so each wall carries four vertices of its own; a solid that looks like one piece is a set of flat pieces that do not share a corner.

chapters.title: The organism: bone, tendon, muscle
chapters.body: A limb of three segments as a parent-child chain with pivots, each joint turning by angle += speed * delta in _process: the course's first body that moves by itself. Beside it, Trans_Body's lattice loses cells where the limb passes.

argument.axis: where the pivot sits on each segment, same joint angles
argument.predict: At rest all four look the same: the pivot moves origins, not bars (measured: no pair differs on more than 0.18% of the frame). With every joint at 30 degrees, one third and the centre are the closest pair, and only the pivot at the end keeps the chain joined: the others open a gap at the knee (5 and 8 cm). Write the pair you expect, at rest and turned, before you render.
argument.claim: A body's motion is decided by where its joints are, not by what its parts look like.

chapters.debt: Klee maps active, medial and passive onto brain, tendon and bone, and onto male and female organs ('Male organs (anthers), active'). The scene tree encodes the same command chain: the parent moves the child, never the reverse. That hierarchy is taught here and inverted in ch21. And frames are not time: speed per frame runs 1.5 times faster at the headset's 90 Hz than at 60 Hz; delta is the repair promised in ch2. Measured in the kit: delta repairs the speed, not the sampling. At 144, 60 and 30 frames a second one turn of the limb carves the same 33 cells; at 3 frames a second it carves 26, because the foot is only asked where it is when a frame comes.

chapters.title: A body of parts: the first assemblage
chapters.body: The parts you have made so far, saved as scenes and instanced into one body: the point (ch2), the cube (ch8), your plane (ch7) and the three-segment limb (ch13), each a PackedScene, each added as a child of one root Node3D with its own pivot. Move the root and every part follows; turn the limb and only the limb's children follow; scale the root and the whole body scales, cube and plane together. The scene tree is the first assemblage: a body is parts in relation, and the tree says which relation.

argument.axis: how the same four parts are parented
values: flat: four children of the root
a chain: each part the child of the one before
argument.predict: At rest all four look the same, and they still look the same when the root turns 30 degrees: every pair differs on 0.00% of the frame, because a root carries everything below it whatever the tree looks like. Turn every pivot 30 degrees and they part: flat and two chains stay closest (0.55% of the frame), the offset chain and two chains are farthest (4.77%), and the toe travels 0.47 m in the flat body against 2.61 m at the end of the chain. Write which pair you expect closest, and when you expect any difference at all, before you render.
argument.claim: The structure of an assemblage is invisible at rest and while only its root moves; it shows when a part inside moves. The tree, not the parts, says what the body does.

chapters.debt: A hierarchy is a command chain. The root moves, the leaves obey, and nothing in the picture shows who commanded whom. Klee drew it as brain, muscle, bone, active to passive; Godot draws it as a tree whose root you chose. The debt is that the choice of root is a choice of who gets to be the body's centre, and the default (the first node you made) is not a neutral one.
chapters.place: Carry the root: pick the whole body up (XR hand or desktop carry) and the parts come with it, pivots and all. Then walk into Trans_Scale with it: the room scales by four, the body scales with the room, and the door you could not use before is usable; the body's relations survive the scale, which is what a hierarchy is for.

chapters.title: The chessboard: purely repetitive and therefore structural
chapters.body: A floor of cubes instanced from a PackedScene in a nested loop. Each cube gets a StandardMaterial3D made in code, coloured by a rule over (x, z): first two colours of your own, then a hue from the index, Color.from_hsv(float(x + z) / (2 * n), s, v).

argument.axis: rhythm rule over the same 8 x 8 cubes
argument.predict: Cell by cell, every cell alike and the x % 3 stripes are the closest pair: they differ in 24 of 64 cells (measured: 11.12% of the frame from the study camera). The chessboard and the stripes disagree on about half the floor (14.26%). Only when the cells are averaged away do the chessboard and the stripes come closest, and that distance was not rendered: it is arithmetic on the stills. The stripes have a direction too: swapping x and z changes 30 of their cells. Write the pair you expect before you render, and say from how far.
argument.claim: Structure is the repetition rule, not the cube: the same 64 bodies make four different floors.

chapters.debt: The grid is the unexamined ground of 3D (editor grids, voxels, the frame buffer as a grid, after Gaboury); it is a choice, and the standing ruling holds that the first line did not need it. HSV promises equal steps of hue, and the eye does not see them as equal: the yellow band looks brighter and wider than the blue one. Measured in the kit: the planted integer division, (x + z) / (2 * n) without float(), gives hue 0 in all 64 cells, a red floor with one warning and no error. One material made before the loops is one material on 64 cubes: change one cube and all 64 change. And the gap a body meets depends on how fast it arrives: a marble let go at 0.75 m passes when the gap equals its width, to the millimetre; dropped from 2 m it passes 2 cm earlier and, just below that, sticks between the cubes. Why it switches where it does is not explained.

chapters.title: Families: one body in a single class
chapters.body: Describe a body in a single class: class_name with two typed @export fields (for a sphere, rings and segments; for your own body, whatever makes it) and a build() function that makes the mesh in _ready(). The supplied sweep sheet instances four members side by side, labelled.

argument.axis: sphere segments (rings = half)
argument.predict: 16 and 64 will look most alike at 2 m (measured: they differ on 0.85% of the still from the side, 0.99% from above, and stay the closest pair lit flat, at 4.65%). Most of that likeness is smooth shading: the rim differs by a band about 3 pixels wide. From above, the outline of 16 misses the circle by 2.06% (the chord arithmetic gives 1.92%). 4 is another body, but not the octahedron: with rings at half it has two rings and 16 triangles. Write the pair you expect, and what you think the likeness is made of, before you render.
argument.claim: The class's integer decides which body you have, and there is no step where a sphere stops paying: against 64 the difference falls evenly, 15.27, 5.17, 0.85, 0.19% for 4, 8, 16 and 32 segments. What looks like enough is a decision about distance and light.

chapters.debt: A class's fields decide which bodies are possible (the CCSWG prompt 'describe it in a single class', turned to a body): an int cannot have 3.5 segments, and no value of rings makes a torus. Polycount against smooth deformation, the application's topology question, enters here. Measured in the kit: set() on a typed int does not refuse a text. It converts it in silence: '16' becomes 16, 'sixteen' becomes 0, '4 8 16 64' becomes 481664, and 640 passes an @export_range of 4 to 64. What set() does refuse in silence is a name the class does not have, and a number handed to a String field. So the planted fault is a wrong field name: four members come back alike under four different plates, and only the printed triangle counts say so (the Ada project's own science_screen case).

chapters.title: The family in the editor: setters, @tool and the sheet opened
chapters.body: Your class with setters that rebuild on change, a rebuild() method, and @tool so the family changes live in the editor (Color_Context_Placed's chroma_stack with its @export_enum rule is the precedent). Then open the supplied sweep sheet and rewrite it yourself, one labelled member per value. For the argument the sheet sweeps Ada's own pyramid (commons/primitives/pyramid/pyramid.gd), whose @export_enum you read rather than retype. pyramid.gd builds its mesh only in _ready(), so the sheet must set apex_stance before add_child(): set it afterwards and nothing changes, which is the reason your own class gets a setter.

argument.axis: where the apex sits over the base: apex_stance, the @export_enum in Ada's pyramid.gd (base 0.6 m, height 0.8 m)
argument.predict: corner and beyond will look most alike. In pyramid.gd's own numbers the apex sits at (0, 0), (0, -0.3), (-0.3, -0.3) and (-0.48, -0.48) in plan: corner and beyond are 0.25 m apart, the closest pair, while centred to edge and edge to corner are 0.30 m apart, and corner and beyond lean along the same diagonal. What the sheet has to show is the one thing the distances do not rank: beyond is the only member whose apex has left its own footprint.
argument.claim: One exported enum carries a pyramid from monument to lean-to, and the step that changes the category is not the largest step.

chapters.debt: The Inspector slider hides what each value costs and what it breaks. Defaults are sacred: an Ada artifact can have hundreds of live placements, so changing a default silently changes every hall it stands in. A setter that rebuilds on every change can stall the editor, and a @tool script runs your bugs inside the editor itself. And the values on your sheet must be read from the code, not typed from memory: a value the class's match does not know falls back to the default without an error, and the sheet shows the same body several times (the Ada DNA programme's science_screen case).

chapters.title: The budget: polycount measured, a claim tested
chapters.body: A parametric surface, the catenoid (u, v) -> point, with exported u_steps and v_steps: you write the two loops over u and v and the SurfaceTool emission, and call a supplied catenoid(u, v) for the point itself (FormFinding_Catenary's formula, with cosh and cos, read now and opened at ch24). Beside it, Primitives_Portals' torus ring, whose segments double while its gap to the true circle is printed and asserted, using the supplied one-liner gap_to_circle(n) = 1 - cos(PI / n).

argument.axis: u_steps of the catenoid
argument.predict: 48 and 96 will look most alike at 2 m: at 48 steps the chord misses the circle by 1 - cos(3.75 deg), about 0.2% of the radius, while 96 costs twice the triangles. The prediction is also written as a test: gap_to_circle(n) < 0.01 passes from n = 24 (0.86%) and fails at 12 (3.4%).
argument.claim: A parametric surface has a step count below which it is a different body and above which it is only cost: the test finds the first, the profiler the second.

chapters.debt: 'Smooth' is a budget decision (application l.89: polycount against deforming a body smoothly), and in a headset at 72-90 Hz every triangle is drawn once per eye. A green test is a fact about the question you asked, not about the body (Montfort: valid and intentional are different).
chapters.place: Stand in it: the catenoid as a neck you walk through at room scale (collider from the mesh). The headset's frame time is the debt you feel: stutter makes people sick, so comfort is not polish.

chapters.title: Collage: a found body joins the family (assemblage II)
chapters.body: Recreate a precedent: the truncated solid of Durer's Melencolia I built as a member of your family, beside a body you scanned (phone photogrammetry in week one) or drew in Tilt Brush or Blender and imported as glTF.

argument.axis: how the body was made
argument.predict: By hand and drafted will look most alike, and here they are the same picture: 0.00% of the still differs from the side, from above and lit flat. The reason is not that they share primitives (one is built with SurfaceTool, the other from an indexed array); the three lines named every number the picture shows. Ask both for a value the lines did not name and they part: a cut of 0.9 is clamped by one and kept by the other, and the stills differ on 14.88%. The found body differs from the solid on about 3% and has 5,851 triangles to its 20. Whether a real scan is the outlier by count and not by silhouette is not tested here: the stand-in was made from the solid, so its outline is near by construction. Write the pair you expect, and what would make two bodies made the same way differ.
argument.claim: Two bodies that look the same have agreed only about what was named. How a body was made shows in what it does with a value nobody asked for, and in its triangle count.

chapters.debt: Recreation (SFPC Recreating the Past): the difference between Durer's solid and yours is where the debt is written; the Melencolia hall already says its hidden surfaces 'are decisions we have made'. The scan has millions of triangles, holes and no inside, and whose bodies scan well is not neutral (Queer 3D: stretchability, topology, bias). Measured in the kit: the import arrives 99.04 m high, its lowest point 4.3 m up and 43 m from its plate, with none of its corners in view. Godot prints no error and still reports the triangle count; the picture shows an empty plate. Scale alone does not bring it home: the file has its own origin, and that is a second fault. The drafted answer in the kit came from one question put once to an assistant of the same kind as the one that wrote the lesson, so it is not an independent witness.

chapters.title: Regions with other laws
chapters.body: An Area3D that replaces gravity with an @export acceleration for any body inside it, the player included, and restores it on exit; your own drag and wind as functions that return force vectors, summed per step (NoC's apply_force).

chapters.title: Pendulum, circle, spiral: time laid into space
chapters.body: A pendulum sampled in _physics_process into a bounded queue and laid out in space as one MultiMesh of marks, so the swing's time becomes a sculpture; then the same runner at (cos t, sin t), a circle; then the radius changes each turn, a spiral starting at 0.5 m.

chapters.debt: A MultiMesh draws thousands of marks in one call and pays in flexibility: every mark shares one mesh and one material. The queue forgets: the sculpture is only the last N samples. And a pendulum that returns forever is an idealisation (the damping you left out).

chapters.title: Displace: a body pushed along its normals by a field

works.note: Perlin noise pushes vertices along their normals
split every face first, then deform: resolution before the push; placed in the reaction-diffusion hall

chapters.body: Take a body you have made and move every vertex along its own normal by the value of a field sampled at that vertex. First by hand, on your own mesh: read its vertices and normals as packed arrays, add normal times noise times an amplitude to each position, generate the normals again, rebuild the collider. Then as the project does it: a MeshGrammar with an icosahedron as its seed and two rules, SplitFaceOp to give the field somewhere to act and NoiseDisplaceOp to push. A sphere under cellular noise becomes a pebble; under a sine it becomes a ripple; your extruded plinth under either stops being an extrusion. Terrain (ch12) lifted a flat grid; this bends any body, and it is the organic half of making form.

argument.axis: how many times the faces are split before the push, same field, seed and amplitude
argument.predict: 2 and 3 splits will look most alike: past a certain density the field is fully drawn and more faces change nothing you can see. With no split the body stays an icosahedron with its corners moved, because the field has almost nowhere to act. Write the pair you expect, and the split at which you think the body stops changing, before you render.
argument.claim: A field can only show where there are vertices to move: resolution is the price of organic form, and it is paid in triangles.

chapters.debt: Polycount against smooth deformation, the application's own sentence, measured on your body. And the blob: bodies displaced by noise resemble each other more than they resemble what they were, so a room of them reads as one aesthetic. Push further than the body's own curvature and the surface passes through itself, which no picture from outside will show you; the marble will.
chapters.place: Grip it: an organic hold. On the desktop, carry it and let the marble settle in its hollows; in the headset, hold it in your hand and turn it. Then put it on the plinth from ch45, a geometric body carrying an organic one.

chapters.title: Same desire: grown bodies join made ones (assemblage V)
chapters.body: One body from three growth rules and one made family. The grammar of ch33 grows the frame; the recursion of ch32 branches it; your family members from ch14 hang on the branches as instanced parts, oriented by the turtle's frame; and the cellular automaton of ch31 decides, row by row, which branches are solid and which are ghosts (ch3's if, now driven by a rule in time). Assemblage_Same_Desire is the hall's own version: one array of small choices, drawn as marks, as paths, and as a floor that carries you. This is also where MeshGrammar, borrowed since ch45, is opened: a rule is a selector, an operation and a dictionary of parameters, and the frame may be grown by it (TubeBranchOp over two generations is the Branching Coral) as well as by your own turtle.

argument.predict: The L-system and the recursive tree will be the closest pair: both branch by angle and shortening, and from the same seed their crowns fill the same volume. The control will be farthest from all three. Write the predicted closest pair, then render the four with the same family hung on them.
argument.claim: The same parts on different frames are different bodies: in an assemblage the growth rule is the body, and the hung family only clothes it.

chapters.debt: Every body a grammar grows looks like the grammar. A rule written in ten lines produces ten thousand branches that all carry its accent, and the accent passes for nature. Who wrote the rule, and what a rule cannot grow (a branch that joins another, a loop, a part that was never a symbol) is the debt; Assemblage_Same_Desire's name says it: the same desire, many paths.

argument.axis: threshold (iso level) of the same field
argument.predict: 0.4 and 0.6 will look most alike: both show separate blobs, one set fatter. At 0.2 the blobs fuse into one body; at 0.8 they shrink into beads.
argument.claim: An implicit body's identity is a threshold: one number decides whether there are three bodies or one.

chapters.debt: The blob aesthetic in its purest form (Queer 3D): metaballs fuse because the field sums them. The lookup table is inherited code nobody in the class wrote, so this chapter holds a code-critique station on Ada's own marching-cubes table (read its comments, find its assumptions). The grid's resolution decides what can be thin.

chapters.title: Combine: union, subtraction, intersection (assemblage VI)
chapters.body: A body carved from your assemblage with three verbs: the union of two family members, the subtraction of the implicit body of ch36 (its tunnel bored through the union), and the intersection with the shell of the scanned body from ch18. CSGCombiner3D holds the operands as children, in order; then the result is baked to a mesh with a collider made from it, because a CSG body is a renderer's interior and physics is told nothing (Boolean_Works' lesson: seventy-five objects offer themselves to your hand and are not there).

argument.axis: the order of the same three operands and verbs
argument.predict: The first two will be the closest pair: they differ only where C overlaps B, so with C's tunnel through A alone they are the same body. The third will lose most of its volume (an intersection keeps only the overlap). Write the predicted closest pair and the volume order, then render.
argument.claim: Boolean combination is not commutative: the order of the verbs is part of the form, and a body carved by subtraction has an inside only where the physics was told so.

chapters.debt: The picture of an inside against an inside. A CSG interior renders perfectly and holds nothing: Boolean_Works hangs 'WALK THE HOLLOW' over a metre of solid rock beneath a cave whose floor is above your head. Baking fixes it at a cost: the seams of a subtraction multiply triangles (polycount against smooth deformation, ch16's debt returns), and the baked mesh forgets its verbs, so the body can no longer be re-carved. An interior is an agreement between the renderer and the physics, and someone has to write it.
chapters.place: Walk into the tunnel before baking and fall through the floor (the hall's own failure, now yours); bake, walk in, and stand in the hollow. Then put the baked body in the museum hall and let a classmate find the seam.

chapters.title: Many bodies with rules: swarms
chapters.body: A flock of your family members as boids: separation, alignment and cohesion as three forces summed per body; each boid joins a group so the others can find it; moved from one node per boid to one MultiMesh when the frame time says so.

argument.axis: cohesion weight (separation and alignment fixed)

argument.claim: A collective body is a ratio of rules: one weight decides whether many bodies are a crowd, a flock or a clump.

chapters.debt: The all-pairs neighbour search costs n squared: a swarm is limited by its budget before it is limited by its rules. Who counts as a neighbour is a radius, a politics of proximity. 'Emergence' is also a way of saying that nobody decided.

chapters.title: Bodies that learn: whose data trains the body
chapters.body: A classifier painted on the floor: labelled points (your ch6 walk traces and classmates', with consent, loaded from a JSON file that records who labelled each one) and a k-nearest-neighbour rule that colours every floor cell by its nearest labels; then a perceptron's line on the same data, and a gradient landscape you walk down.

argument.axis: who labelled the training points
argument.predict: The class and the default dataset will look most alike: smooth, confident regions. Random labels give a speckled field, and your own labels draw the most particular map.
argument.claim: The decision field is a map of who labelled the data: the machine's confidence is borrowed from its labellers.

chapters.debt: Models are always biased (Queer 3D 2024), and raising k erases the lone sample's region (k as a politics of neighbourhood). The course's own AI assistant (ch8) was trained on labels nobody in the room chose: ask it for 'a human body' and study what it returns. A test proves only what you thought to ask: the perceptron fails XOR.
chapters.place: Stand on your own portrait: the field under your feet says which class your position belongs to; walk across the boundary the data drew.

chapters.title: The crisis of foundations: impossible possible space
chapters.body: An impossible figure that exists from one standpoint only: a Penrose triangle of three straight beams that closes when your camera reaches the one point (the figure emits viewpoint_locked and the room awaits it); and a corridor whose curvature is a shader uniform, so parallel lines meet.

argument.axis: the viewer's distance from the locked standpoint
argument.predict: 0.5 and 2 m will look most alike: both plainly show three separate beams. 0 is the only closed triangle; 0.1 already shows a hairline gap.
argument.claim: An impossible body is a possible body seen from one place: the impossibility is in the standpoint, not in the geometry.

chapters.debt: Mathematics has 'limits and areas of unpredictability and undecidability' (Queer 3D: Godel, the halting problem): no test suite can prove a program halts. Brouwer's third value as enum Truth {TRUE, FALSE, NOT_YET} (c1): allowing 'not yet' is a political choice. Failure before futures: the course names what its models cannot hold before it builds its own hall.
chapters.place: Find the standpoint: walk until the figure closes, take one step and watch it break; walk the curved corridor until you come back to where you began.

chapters.title: Order toward entropy: the QFEP laboratory
chapters.body: Your own prediction log becomes a body: every prediction and observation you wrote since ch2, loaded from your sketchbook, with F = |prediction - observation| per chapter drawn as a line you walk along (a heuristic reading of QFEP's F term: a prediction error you wrote down, not a measured free energy). Beside it, 200 seeded symbols sorted by a tween while their Shannon entropy is counted (Random_Entropy).

argument.axis: how the same 200 symbols are arranged
argument.predict: 'sorted by value' and 'reversed' will look most alike: they are mirror images. All four carry exactly the same counted entropy: the picture changes and the number does not.
argument.claim: Entropy counts what there is, not how it is arranged: order is a picture, not a quantity.

chapters.debt: Shannon entropy measures a distribution and is blind to arrangement: the metric hides exactly what a visual argument shows. QFEP is the project's own framework, and the F term measured on the course's learners must not become a score (c2's warning): the log is for the student, not for the grade. The entropy counted here is the Shannon entropy of the symbol frequencies in one row, a stated distribution and a stated estimator. It is not the entropy of the room, of your search or of you, and the chapter makes no claim about those.
chapters.place: Walk your own F curve: the chapters where your prediction was most wrong are the highest points; stand on them.

chapters.title: Out of the lab: your hall in the collective museum (assemblage VII, final)
chapters.body: Your hall in Ada's endless museum, built from your families, each body with its prediction, comparison sheet, claim and debt comment; one public sculpture whose visitors' changes are kept as provenance records (who, when, what) in files under user://, readable by the next visitor; exported to desktop and Quest.

argument.axis: who may change the sculpture
argument.predict: 'only the author' and 'sealed' will look most alike in any still: to a visitor both are unchanging. Last write wins drifts toward the latest visitor, and kept history grows layers.
argument.claim: A public body is its edit rule: who may revise it, and whether revisions are kept, shows in its shape over a week.

chapters.debt: Can the work keep its conditions, exclusions and possible revisions available to others (the post-crisis question)? Illich's repairability and the application's commoning: a hall that can be opened and changed. Collective memory is also surveillance: the provenance log records its visitors, so it asks for consent at the door.
chapters.place: Show it: the hall stands in the class's shared museum, where classmates walk, carry, revise or become its bodies, on desktop and in the headset.
